You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Bitget UEX Daily｜Trump Says US Will Strike Iran Hard; Fed Holds Rates Steady as Warsh Reaffirms 2% Target; Microsoft Beats on Cloud While Meta Raises Capex (July 30, 2026)

TEXT:
I. Hot News Highlights
Federal Reserve Developments
Fed Holds Rates Steady; Warsh Reaffirms 2% Inflation Target and Downplays Forward Guidance
The Federal Reserve kept interest rates unchanged. In his opening remarks at the press conference, Chair Warsh clearly restated that the Committee remains firmly committed to the 2% year-over-year inflation target and that there is no “soft target” or any other implicit objective.
Warsh said that in the current highly uncertain environment, providing no forward guidance is a prudent approach. Markets have independently priced in tighter monetary policy expectations; the Fed will monitor developments closely but will not passively follow market pricing.
After the decision, CME data showed the probability of holding rates steady in September rising to 36.8%, with a 63.2% chance of a cumulative 25 bp hike.
Market Impact : Policy path uncertainty persists. Hawkish signals coexist with a “hold,” supporting the dollar in the near term, pressuring risk-asset valuations, and reinforcing pricing of sticky inflation.
International Commodities
Trump Says US Will Strike Iran Hard; Military Prepares Up to Two-Week Intensive Airstrike Plan
At the White House, Trump stated that because Iran fired missiles at US forces in the Middle East, the United States “will give Iran a heavy blow” and that “it is now America’s turn to strike back.” He added that Iran knows the strike is inevitable and has asked the US not to proceed.
US media reported that US Central Command has prepared a punitive intensive airstrike plan lasting up to 10–14 days aimed at degrading Iran’s missile capabilities, pending Trump’s final decision. The military has simultaneously warned that air-defense munitions stocks are running low.
Trump is also seeking authority to impose tariffs on Iran in related sanctions legislation.
Market Impact : Expectations of renewed geopolitical escalation rapidly lifted the crude risk premium. Oil prices rebounded significantly, intensifying the inflation–Fed policy tug-of-war and keeping market sen time nt highly sensitive.
Macroeconomic Policy
Treasury May Delay Adjusting Debt Issuance Guidance; Political Factors Dominate
JPMorgan strategists believe the US Treasury, to avoid unsettling the bond market ahead of the midterm elections, is likely to leave its wording unchanged in next week’s quarterly refunding statement and postpone any signal of larger Treasury issuance.
The US faces an estimated $3.7 trillion financing gap over the next four fiscal years, yet political considerations may take priority over pure debt-management objectives.
Market Impact : Long-term Treasury yields are already near the highest levels since Trump took office. The interplay of policy and politics increases volatility across fixed income and risk assets.
II. Market Recap
Commodities & FX Performance
Spot Gold : ~$4,081/oz, +0.37%
Spot Silver : ~$58/oz, +1.55%
WTI Crude : ~$84/bbl, +0.06%
Brent Crude : ~$83/bbl, significant 24h gains
US Dollar Index (DXY) : ~100.9, +0.08%
Driver Analysis : Trump’s “strike Iran hard” remarks and the disclosure of a multi-week US airstrike plan quickly elevated the geopolitical risk premium, supporting crude prices. Gold and silver showed mixed performance amid rising oil prices and post-Fed divergence, with overall safe-haven demand remaining limited. The dollar stayed relatively firm, reflecting lingering policy uncertainty. The linkage is clear: renewed geopolitical escalation → higher oil → rising inflation concerns → elevated Fed hawkish odds. Near-term commodity volatility will depend heavily on developments in the Iran situation and upcoming economic data.
Cryptocurrency Performance
BTC : ~$63,718, -0.17%
ETH : ~$1,900, -0.52%
Total Crypto Market Cap : ~$2.28 trillion, -0.1%
Liquidations (24h) : Total ~$389 million, of which longs ~$270 million
Bitget BTC/ USDT Liquidation Map : Liquidation pressure is limited near the current price (~$63,782). The $64,700–$65,300 zone contains a dense cluster of 50x and 100x short liquidations. A break above this area could trigger concentrated short covering and amplify upside momentum. Cumulative short liquidation size above (~$500 million) exceeds long liquidation size below (~$440 million), so short-side risk remains dominant and short-squeeze potential is higher in the near term, though resistance around the high-leverage zone near $65,000 warrants attention.
Spot ETF Flows : BTC spot ETFs recorded a net outflow of approximately $50 million yesterday and a dynamic net outflow of about $58 million today, marking five consecutive days of outflows.

However, oil-price strength driven by geopolitical tensions and inflation concerns continue to act as a macro headwind. Lighter liquidation pressure has helped stabilize prices, while cautious ETF flows show institutions remain on the sidelines. The overall trend is range-bound with a mild constructive bias; near-term focus shifts to Apple and Amazon earnings as well as developments on the Iran front.

Chip and memory stocks sold off sharply—Micron fell nearly 10%, AMD and Intel dropped more than 5%, and Nvidia declined more than 3%—dragging the Nasdaq lower. AI application software remained strong, with Adobe up nearly 6% and Workday and others gaining more than 5%. Apple and Microsoft were relatively resilient, while Google rose against the trend. Microsoft surged in after-hours trading on strong cloud results, underscoring the market’s preference for “earnings delivery.” The overall pattern remains hardware under pressure while software and selected mega-cap tech hold up better, reflecting ongoing re-pricing of AI capital-expenditure returns.
